HIIT vs LISS: which cardio is better for fat loss?

High-intensity intervals are sold as the fat-burning shortcut; steady walking and cycling are sold as the gentle, sustainable option. Both work. The better choice depends on your time, your recovery and how much you lift.

By Khushi Gupta · Reviewed October 2026 · 5 min read

The two types, defined

HIIT (high-intensity interval training) alternates short, hard efforts with recovery. A typical session is 6 to 10 rounds of 20 to 60 seconds hard, with equal or longer easy periods, totalling 15 to 25 minutes including warm-up.

LISS (low-intensity steady state) is continuous work at an easy to moderate pace: brisk walking, easy cycling, rowing or swimming for 30 to 60 minutes. You can hold a conversation throughout.

Between them sits moderate-intensity continuous training, such as a steady 30-minute jog, which many studies use as the comparison.

HIITLISS
Heart rate85-95% of max in work intervals60-70% of max
Session length15-25 minutes30-60+ minutes
Sessions per week1-33-7
Recovery costHighLow
Skill or fitness neededModerate base fitnessAlmost none

Use the heart rate zone calculator to find your own numbers.

What the research says about fat loss

Head-to-head studies show that both approaches reduce body fat, and the difference between them is small. A meta-analysis by Wewege et al. (Obesity Reviews, 2017) found that interval training and moderate continuous training produced similar reductions in body fat, with intervals taking roughly 40 percent less time.

Some later analyses, such as Viana et al. (British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2019), reported a modestly greater fat loss with interval training, particularly sprint intervals. Even there, the absolute differences were small compared with the effect of diet.

The so-called afterburn (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) is real but modest, usually adding only a few dozen extra calories, not the hundreds often claimed.

Fat loss is also not the only reason to do cardio. The World Health Organization recommends adults get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, each week, alongside muscle strengthening on two or more days. Both HIIT and LISS count towards that, and both improve heart health, blood pressure and blood sugar control.

Cardio supports fat loss; your calorie deficit drives it. Set that first with the calorie calculator, then choose cardio you will keep doing.

Calories burned: a realistic comparison

Per minute, HIIT burns more. Per session, longer steady cardio often matches or beats it, because you can do much more of it. Rough figures for a 75 kg (165 lb) person:

SessionDurationApprox. calories
Brisk walk, 6 km/h45 min250-300
Easy cycling45 min300-400
Steady jog, 9 km/h30 min330-380
Bike sprint intervals20 min incl. warm-up200-280
Rowing intervals20 min incl. warm-up220-300

Estimates vary with fitness and body size. Get a figure for your own weight with the calories burned calculator.

How each affects your lifting

Cardio and strength training compete for recovery. This is called the interference effect, and it is strongest when cardio is high-impact, high-volume, and done close to leg training.

  • HIIT is demanding on the legs and nervous system. Two or three sessions a week can eat into squat and deadlift performance if placed badly.
  • LISS, especially walking or cycling, has little effect on lifting and may help recovery.
  • Running has more impact than cycling or rowing, so it interferes more with leg training.

If muscle and strength are your priority, lean towards LISS and keep HIIT to one or two short sessions. Separate hard cardio from leg days by at least 24 hours, or do it after lifting rather than before.

Don't overlook steps

Non-exercise activity, such as walking around, taking stairs and standing, often burns more calories across a week than formal cardio. It also tends to drop without you noticing when you diet, which is one reason fat loss slows.

A daily step target is the simplest form of LISS. Moving from 4,000 to 9,000 steps a day can add roughly 200 to 300 calories of daily burn for many people, with almost no recovery cost.

Who should choose which

SituationBetter choice
Short on timeHIIT, 2 x 20 minutes a week
Beginner or very deconditionedLISS; build a base first
Heavy lifting 4+ days a weekMostly LISS, max 1 HIIT
Joint pain or high bodyweightLISS on bike, rower or in water
Want better fitness (VO2 max)Mix both
Deep in a diet, low energyLISS and steps

Ask your doctor before starting HIIT if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, or have been inactive for a long time.

Most people end up doing best with a mix: plenty of easy movement as the base, plus a small dose of hard intervals once fitness allows. The easy work burns calories and aids recovery; the intervals build fitness quickly and keep sessions short.

Whatever you choose, judge it after six to eight weeks by your weekly average weight, waist measurement and how your lifting is going, not by how exhausted a single session leaves you.

A weekly plan that combines both

This template works alongside three or four lifting sessions, for example the fat loss workout plan or an upper lower split:

DayLiftingCardio
MonUpper20-30 min walk
TueLowerNone or easy walk
WedRest40-45 min LISS
ThuUpper15-20 min HIIT after lifting
FriLower20-30 min walk
SatRest45-60 min LISS
SunRestEasy walk

Plus a daily step target of 7,000 to 10,000. Start with less if you are new and add one session every week or two.

Choosing the best LISS for you

The best steady cardio is the one you will do three to five times a week without dreading it or getting hurt. Each option has a different trade-off:

ActivityJoint impactLeg fatigueNotes
Walking (incl. incline)Very lowVery lowEasiest to fit into daily life
Cycling (outdoor or stationary)Very lowLow to moderateGood for heavier people
SwimmingNoneLowTechnique limits intensity for beginners
Rowing machineLowModerateWorks the whole body
EllipticalLowLowEasy to hold a steady heart rate
JoggingHighModerate to highBuild up mileage slowly

Incline treadmill walking deserves a mention: at a 10 to 12 percent incline and a moderate pace, it pushes your heart rate up without the impact of running, and it barely touches your lifting recovery.

Common cardio mistakes

  • Eating it back: fitness trackers often overestimate calories burned, and many people eat more after cardio. Do not add cardio calories back to your diet unless you are losing weight faster than planned.
  • Doing HIIT too often: intervals done four or five times a week stop being high intensity. Quality drops and fatigue builds.
  • All grey-zone effort: many people do every session at a medium-hard pace that is neither easy enough to recover from nor hard enough to count as intervals. Make easy days easy and hard days hard.
  • Starting too big: going from zero to an hour a day leads to sore joints and quitting. Add 10 to 15 minutes per week.
  • Replacing lifting with cardio: while dieting, lifting is what tells your body to keep muscle. Keep it in.

A simple HIIT session to start with

  1. Warm up for 5 minutes at an easy pace on a bike or rower.
  2. Go hard for 30 seconds, at roughly 8 out of 10 effort.
  3. Recover for 90 seconds at an easy pace.
  4. Repeat 6 times. Add a round every week up to 10.
  5. Cool down for 5 minutes.

Bikes and rowers are safer for intervals than sprinting, which has a higher injury risk if you have not sprinted in years. As fitness improves, shorten recovery to 60 seconds before adding rounds.

Frequently asked questions

Is HIIT better than walking for fat loss?

Per minute, HIIT burns more calories, but walking can be done daily for long periods with almost no fatigue. Over a week, both lead to similar fat loss when diet is the same.

Does cardio kill muscle gains?

Moderate amounts do not, especially low-impact cardio like walking or cycling. Large volumes of running or hard intervals close to leg sessions can reduce strength and muscle gains.

How many times a week should I do HIIT?

One to three sessions is plenty. More than that adds fatigue that can hurt your lifting and raises injury risk.

Should I do cardio before or after weights?

If strength or muscle is your priority, lift first. Light cardio as a warm-up is fine, but hard cardio before lifting reduces performance.

Is fasted cardio better for burning fat?

Fasted cardio burns a higher proportion of fat during the session, but studies show no extra fat loss over time when daily calories are equal. Choose whichever timing you prefer.
